title: Corruption Perceptions, the Pendleton Act, and Sovereign Borrowing Costs
authors: John A. Dove; Noah J. Trudeau
affiliations: School of Creative Enterprise and Market Systems, Sorrell College of Business Troy University Troy Alabama USA
abstract: ABSTRACT Significant research suggests that systems of bureaucratic patronage tend to promote corruption and reduce the efficient production of publicly provided goods. However, much less work has been done to consider how market actors perceive such selection processes and especially reforms implemented to reduce such corruption. This study rectifies this by evaluating how the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act impacted federal borrowing costs. If patronage resulted in increased corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency, this should be reflected in relatively higher bond yields. If the Pendleton Act was successful in curbing this behavior, then this should be rewarded by market actors in the form of lower borrowing costs. Using interrupted time series analysis with and without control, we find that the passage of the Pendleton Act did, in fact, result in lower borrowing costs for the federal government of between 63 and 84 basis points depending on specification. Implications are discussed.

title: Supplemental Material for Revisiting the Assumption of a Self-Regulatory Loop: A Cross-Lagged Study of the Relationship Between Role Ambiguity and Feedback Seeking
Spoofing and Manipulating Order Books with Learning Algorithms
authors: Alvaro Cartea; Patrick Chang; Gabriel Garcia Arenas
affiliations: University of Oxford, Mathematics, Oxford, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Oxford, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
abstract: We propose a dynamic model of the limit order book to derive conditions to test whether it is optimal to manipulate the order book. Our results show that as a market maker becomes more tolerant to bearing inventory risk, optimal strategies that manipulate the book occur more frequently. Manipulation helps to revert inventory to an optimal level and to execute round-trip trades with limit orders at a higher probability than was otherwise likely to occur. Spoofing is a special case of quote-based manipulation where the market maker prefers that the manipulative limit orders are not filled. Overall, if certain conditions hold, then the optimal trading strategy is to manipulate the limit order book. We use high-frequency data to check our conditions and show that the conditions for manipulation hold in Nasdaq’s limit order book.

title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
authors: Guanhao Feng; Liang Jiang; Junye Li; Yizhi Song; Yuanzhi Wang
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, Kowloon 999077, Hong Kong SAR; International School of Finance, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China; School of Management, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China; International Business School, Hainan University, Haikou 570228, China; University of Science and Technology of China, Hefei 230026, China
abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. title: Learning from a Biased Sample
authors: Roshni Sahoo; Lihua Lei; Stefan Wager
affiliations: Columbia Business School, Columbia University, New York 10027; Graduate School of Business, Stanford University, Palo Alto, California 94305
abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. We empirically validate our proposed method in a case study on prediction of mental health scores from health survey data and a case study on intensive care unit length-of-stay prediction. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: This research was supported by NSF grant SES-2242876. title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
authors: Chen Chen; Pengyu Qian; Jingwei Zhang
affiliations: New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China; Questrom School of Business, Boston University, Boston, Massachusetts 02215; School of Data Science, School of Management and Economics, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangdong 518172, China
abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. This paper was accepted by Peng Sun, optimization and decision analytics. Funding: J. title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
authors: Lin Nan; Lin Qiu; Xiaoyan Wen; Ronghuo Zheng
affiliations: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana 47907; Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, Texas 76129; University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712
abstract: This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
authors: Diego Aparicio; Duncan I. Simester
affiliations: Georgetown University, Washington, District of Columbia 20057; MIT Sloan School of Management, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02142
abstract: We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02602 .

title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
authors: Zhongbin Wang; Shiliang Cui; Yongjian Li; Qian Zhang
affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University, Tianjin 300072, China; McDonough School of Business, Georgetown University, Washington, District of Columbia 20057; Business School, Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, China; School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710049, China
abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. title: Understanding the Prompting Effects of Chain-of-Thought on Human Collaboration with Generative AI
authors: Xusen Cheng; Lu Gao; Qiguang Yang; Xin (Robert) Luo
affiliations: Renmin University of China, School of Information, Beijing, China; Renmin University of China, School of Journalism and Communication, Beijing, China; Hong Kong Metropolitan University, Lee Shau Kee School of Business and Administration, Hong Kong, Hong Kong
abstract: It is well established that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves model performance in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Far less understood is whether presenting CoT reasoning in AI-enabled interfaces enhances users’ perceived trust in GenAI’s competence in performing tasks. Drawing on the Heuristic-Systematic Model, we develop a theoretical framework in which CoT presence and quality trigger either heuristic perceptions of transparency or systematic perceptions of diagnosticity and germane cognitive load, with distinct mechanisms across task-difficulty conditions. Across a series of online experiments, we identify two key findings. First, high-quality CoT consistently enhances perceived trust in GenAI’s ability to generate correct outputs, regardless of task difficulty. Notably, under high-difficulty conditions, users’ trust in GenAI is primarily driven by the greater germane cognitive load perceived from high-quality CoT, whereas under low-difficulty conditions, trust is primarily driven by perceived transparency or diagnosticity. Second, low-quality CoT reduces users’ competence trust in GenAI that generates incorrect outputs only under low-difficulty conditions and only when users engage in careful processing, operating through perceived diagnosticity. Yet, under high-difficulty conditions, low-quality CoT amplifies trust via perceived transparency. By disentangling the cognitive pathways through which CoT shapes competence trust in GenAI and by identifying task difficulty as a critical boundary condition, these findings deepen our understanding of transparent reasoning in AI interfaces and offer valuable insights for deploying CoT in GenAI systems.

title: Short-horizon capital in a bank-centered financial system: Japanese mutual fund launches relative to the U.S.
authors: Toshiki Honda; Alan Guoming Huang; Daisuke Miyakawa; Sho Nishiuchi; Russ Wermers
abstract: Abstract The median time from launch to peak assets under management (AUM) is nine months for Japanese active domestic equity mutual funds, versus 4.6 years for comparable U.S. funds. Japanese funds also grow much less from launch to peak, as strong initial inflows quickly give way to persistent outflows, while U.S. funds continue to attract net inflows for years. We link this compressed life cycle to Japan’s bank-centered, concentrated distribution system and front-loaded sales compensation. A larger launch size and higher sales load each predict earlier peak AUM in Japan, but not in the U.S.; within Japan, stronger distribution networks are associated with larger launches and earlier peaks, while longer pre-inception sales periods are associated with larger launch sizes and higher sales loads. The evidence shows that the same market-based financial product can follow different life cycles when embedded in different national systems of intermediation and compensation. Japan’s prolonged weak equity-market environment provides an additional context in which investors may reassess newly launched funds as realized performance becomes observable. Our findings suggest that incentives rewarding initial sales can mobilize capital rapidly without generating durable asset retention in an institutional environment such as Japan’s.

title: Adapting to the new abnormal: multinational corporations’ foreign subsidiary investment and country resilience to climate change
authors: Chang Hoon Oh; Jorge Rivera; Jennifer Oetzel
abstract: Abstract As climate change (CC) increasingly disrupts infrastructure, supply chains, labor availability, and public services, multinational corporations (MNCs) face growing uncertainty when selecting locations for foreign expansion. We examine whether host-country CC resilience has become an important determinant of international investment and how firm capabilities shape this relationship. Drawing on socio-ecological resilience theory and the resilience and turbulence framework, we analyze Global Fortune 500 firms investing across 155 countries between 2003 and 2017. We find that MNCs establish more wholly owned subsidiaries in countries with higher CC resilience, indicating that resilience is emerging as a strategic location-specific advantage. This relationship is stronger for firms with well-developed ESG capabilities and prior experience operating in resilient countries, but weaker for firms with greater financial slack. Our findings suggest that managers should incorporate CC resilience into location decisions alongside traditional economic and institutional criteria while considering their firms’ resource and capability profile to assess how effectively they can leverage host-country CC resilience. For policymakers, the results indicate that strengthening CC resilience can improve not only adaptation to CC but also national competitiveness in attracting MNC foreign direct investment. Overall, CC resilience is becoming a strategic determinant of where MNCs choose to invest.

title: Educational gradients of housework and childcare time in East Asian and Anglophone countries from the 1980s to the 2020s
authors: Matthew Henglong Luo; Grace Chang; Man-Yee Kan
affiliations: University of Oxford, UK
abstract: The past half-century witnessed substantial changes in both behaviours and ideologies concerning the division of labour and child-rearing. This study aims to examine how educational attainment is associated with housework and childcare time for both men and women, how these patterns have evolved from the 1980s to the 2020s, and whether the evolution differs between East Asian and Anglophone countries. Using time-diary data from two East Asian countries (Japan and South Korea) and three Anglophone countries (the USA, the UK, and Canada), our analyses reveal that (a) education promotes gender convergence in housework contributions; (b) higher-educated parents generally spend more time on childcare; (c) educational gaps in housework are relatively stable over time, while educational gaps in childcare increase over time; (d) the trends differ between East Asian and Anglophone countries in terms of the evolution stage. These findings are discussed regarding the implications for gender revolution and intergenerational stratification.

title: ‘The dutiful mum thing’: Family solidarity in the context of Turner Syndrome
authors: Kriss Fearon
affiliations: De Montfort University, Leicester, UK
abstract: Intrafamilial egg donation enables an infertile woman to have a genetically-linked child using eggs from a female relative. This practice provides a lens to scrutinise current practices of family solidarity; the social expectation that family members will support each other. Families affected by Turner Syndrome, a chromosome condition usually resulting in infertility, offer a unique perspective on how perceptions of family solidarity influence attitudes to intrafamilial donation. This article explores attitudes to sister and maternal egg donation, drawn from a qualitative study exploring reproductive choices in 19 women with Turner Syndrome and 11 mothers of girls with Turner Syndrome. It shows how reproductive technologies can reshape expectations about family solidarity and maternal responsibility, demonstrating the delicate balance between creating genetically-connected family and maintaining family harmony.

title: Visualizing Uncertainty in Dispersion Forecasting: Effects on User Perceptions and Communication
authors: Helen Miller; Susan Leadbetter; Sarah C. Jenkins
affiliations: Met Office Exeter UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Operational dispersion forecasts have traditionally been produced deterministically, producing a single best estimate of the situation despite inherent uncertainty. Recently, there has been a paradigmatic shift toward providing uncertainty information as part of operational aviation forecasts. Yet, little is currently known about how exactly this information should be presented or about its effects on understanding and perceptions (vs. purely deterministic information). Using an ensemble of dispersion forecasts (produced using varying inputs) allows visualization of some of the dispersion uncertainty. Here, we compared how deterministic versus ensemble visualizations affected the graphical and written guidance provided. Across two scenarios featuring volcanic eruptions, 30 participants working in atmospheric dispersion were asked to produce an advisory graphic (a polygon encompassing an area of volcanic ash) and a written statement, as well as to rate the visualizations for utility, clarity, and importance. Overall, we find that participants drew bigger polygons (encompassing a larger geographical extent) in the uncertain, ensemble condition, though these were more consistent than those in the deterministic condition. Advisory statements in the ensemble condition also reflected greater uncertainty. Broadly, perceptions of the uncertainty information were neutral to positive, though graphics where less ash was shown were perceived as less useful. Our findings indicate that the presence of uncertainty information can influence communication products generated, underlining the importance of testing ensemble visualizations with users.

title: Elections, Expert Assessments and Public Sector Leaks: Evidence From a Survey Experiment
authors: Zuzana Murdoch; Benny Geys
affiliations: Department of Government University of Bergen Bergen Norway; Department of Economics BI Norwegian Business School Bergen Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite strong normative, professional and legal constraints, leaks of confidential information by public administrators continue to arise. Yet, data limitations restrict our knowledge about when such actions are most/least likely. Conceptualizing the decision to leak confidential information as a “bureaucratic dilemma,” we theorize that this decision is affected by election proximity and positive/negative expert assessments of policy proposals. We test the resulting theoretical propositions via a between‐subjects survey experiment among 1661 national public administrators in Norway. Our results reveal that impending elections reduce the perceived probability of leaks among public administrators who support government parties, while having the reverse effect among public administrators not supporting government parties. We also uncover that leaks become less—not more—likely when there is a negative expert assessment of a policy proposal (relative to a control group receiving no expert assessment). Our findings help elucidate the information‐sharing dilemmas faced by public administrators.

title: Small N, High Stakes: Simulating Adverse Impact With Bayesian Logistic Regression Analysis and Permutation Tests
authors: Patrick J. Rolwes; Karyssa A. Courey; Frederick L. Oswald; Michelle P. Martín-Raugh
affiliations: The University of Texas at Arlington; Louisiana State University; University of California
abstract: Organizations frequently evaluate adverse impact with rules of thumb and statistical tests that perform poorly when hiring cohorts are small, raising scientific concerns that have legal and ethical implications. To address these concerns, this study conducts Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests as two new approaches to conducting adverse impact analysis under small-sample conditions. Simulations were varied across a realistic range of effect sizes, selection rates, and group sample sizes. The performance of each method was evaluated in terms of Type I error rates and statistical power. Results indicated that both Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests are viable alternatives to traditional methods under small-sample conditions. Bayesian odds-ratio rules with noninformative or weakly informative priors in particular demonstrated higher power than frequentist methods at small sample sizes, although no method reached .80 power on average. Their Type I error rates sometimes exceeded the nominal .05 level but remained well below those of the 4/5ths rule. Implications and advantages of each method are discussed in detail.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Consumer Fairness Seeking in Live-Stream E-Commerce
authors: Baozhuang Niu; Jianhua Zhang; Qiyang Li; Xinhu Yu; Yulan Wang
abstract: As live-stream e-commerce rapidly expands and gains popularity among consumers, many brand owners have supplemented their self-owned direct-selling channels with live-stream selling channels to utilize social network effects of key opinion leaders (KOLs). This dual-channel structure creates price discrepancy issues, prompting consumers to raise concerns about price fairness. Therefore, brand owners are motivated to coordinate pricing strategies, balancing cooperation and competition across channels. We build a game-theoretical model to investigate how consumers' peer-induced fairness seeking influences the price decisions of a brand owner (in the direct-selling channel) and the KOL (in the live-stream selling channel). Interestingly, we find that consumers' increased fairness concerns may paradoxically lead to increased prices in both channels, challenging the conventional expectation of price-cutting competition. We further demonstrate that consumers' fairness seeking may either benefit or harm both sellers, depending on the strength of network effects and various factors related to competition intensity. The non-monotonic impacts of consumer fairness seeking are driven by the brand owner's dueling strategic incentives to secure (or relinquish) its direct-selling business to compete with (or favor) the live-stream selling under different situations. Finally, we identify “win-win”, “lose-lose”, and “lose-win” outcomes that consumer fairness seeking can cause for the brand owner and KOL.

title: EXPRESS: Supercharging the Confidence Trap: Too-Big-to-Fail and Man-Made Disasters
authors: Akhil Bhardwaj; Henk Akkermans; Luk N. Van Wassenhove
abstract: Man-made disasters are always shocking, especially when they involve loss of life. The shock is even greater when such disasters are attributed to failures in highly regulated organizations like Boeing, long known for engineering excellence and safety. In the spirit of pragmatic inquiry that considers attenuating the likelihood of disasters an urgent and important problem, we explore the underlying dynamics that can lead to such outcomes. We draw on an agent-based modelling approach within a system dynamics framework. We argue that operational and organizational complexity creates barriers to identifying failures that contribute to disasters. A key contributor to this dynamic is the weakening of regulatory oversight, as both regulators and operators fall into a “confidence trap” – a mistaken belief that past risk-taking success justifies continued risk-taking. This dynamic is exacerbated when the organization in question is perceived as “too big to fail,” which shields it from market selection mechanisms. To mitigate these factors, we propose two policy levers. First, we propose financial clawbacks that require executives to return part of their compensation in the event of a disaster. This aligns incentives of the regulator and executives by injecting the latter’s “skin in the game,” and attenuates the moral hazard problem. Second, we propose third-party monitoring and auditing that serve to mitigate regulatory oversight and better utilize expertise. Simulations indicate these levers significantly reduce the likelihood and impact of failures that lead to disasters, offering a robust logic of pursuit.

title: The Reversal of the Gender Gap in Automation: Evidence From the US Labor Market
authors: Montserrat Martí; Alejandro Micco; Francisca Pérez
affiliations: Department of Economics Brown University Providence Rhode Island USA; Faculty of Economics and Business University of Chile Santiago Chile; Business School Adolfo Ibáñez University Santiago Chile
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper documents a reversal in the US gender gap in the probability of automation, 1976–2019. Women initially had higher automation probabilities than men, but the gap narrowed and reversed. The aggregate change occurs mainly within sectors, from clerical and retail sales to professional and technical occupations. The reversal is associated with education and occupational work‐hour structure. It is concentrated among newer cohorts: cohort‐specific gaps absorb most of the trend and attenuate as education, work‐hour structure, and social skills are added. These patterns are consistent with broad changes in women's occupational conditions but do not identify their causal mechanisms.

title: Beyond Union Membership: Wage Formation and Collective Institutions
authors: Fredrik B. Kostøl; Elin W. Svarstad
affiliations: Department of Industrial Economics and Technology Management Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) Trondheim Norway; Fafo Institute of Labour and Social Research Oslo Norway
abstract: ABSTRACT Using linked Norwegian employer‐employee register data for 2016–2023, we examine how union membership, workplace union density, and collective agreement coverage relate to wages. Union membership, workplace union density, and collective agreement coverage represent distinct dimensions of collective presence and should not be treated as conceptually equivalent. We find that union members earn more than non‐members irrespective of coverage, while the relationship between wages and union density depends on membership and coverage. Collective agreements are not associated with a uniform wage premium. However, covered firms have smaller white‐collar wage premia and a weaker relationship between wages and productivity for white‐collar workers.

title: Knowledge‐Based Industry Sectoral Regimes and Internal Labour Flexibility: The Visibility and Adjustment of Overtime During Systemic Disruption in the United Kingdom
authors: Ramin Taghinejad; Ali Intezari; Peyman Akhavan; Adam Pawliczek
affiliations: Faculty of Management Prague University of Economics and Business Jindřichův Hradec Czech Republic; UQ Business School, Faculty of Business, Economics and Law The University of Queensland Brisbane Queensland Australia; London College of Contemporary Arts Global University Systems London UK; Department of Management Moravian Business College Olomouc Olomouc Czech Republic
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how firms adjust labour input during economic disruptions requires attention not only to employment changes but also to the internal mechanisms through which work is reorganised. Although industrial relations research distinguishes between internal and external labour flexibility, less is known about how industry sectoral regimes are associated with observable differences in internal working‐time adjustment. This study examines whether manufacturing and knowledge‐intensive services (KIS) differ in their reliance on recorded paid overtime as an observable form of internal working‐time adjustment and whether this difference changes during systemic disruption. Using UK regional panel data from 2016 to 2025, we measure overtime dependence (OD) as the ratio of paid overtime hours to total paid hours. Fixed‐effects models with region and year effects examine sectoral differences, whereas dynamic specifications assess persistence in overtime utilisation. The analysis focuses on the 2020–2021 COVID‐19 period, with alternative periods used for robustness analysis. The results show that manufacturing exhibits substantially higher OD than KIS, but this difference narrows significantly during the 2020–2021 systemic disruption period, driven primarily by a sharper contraction in manufacturing OD. Alternative temporal specifications provide additional evidence on the timing and robustness of this change. Lower recorded paid overtime in KIS should not be interpreted as lower labour flexibility, because adjustment may occur through alternative mechanisms not observed in the present data. The study contributes to industrial relations research by conceptualising recorded paid overtime as an observable indicator of one internal working‐time adjustment margin rather than a comprehensive measure of labour flexibility.

title: Coming Clean on Hidden Ties: How Transparency in Related‐Party Transactions Shapes Business Group Internal Organization
authors: Marina Gama; Rodrigo DeMello; Aldo Musacchio; Tobias Parente
affiliations: São Paulo School of Business Administration (FGV‐SP); Bentley University; Brandeis University; University of São Paulo (PPGA/FEA‐USP)
abstract: Abstract This study demonstrates that transparency reforms trigger organizational restructuring within pyramidal business groups rather than simply eliminating opacity. Building on pyramidal ownership theory, we argue that enhanced disclosure alters the relative value of security benefits and diversion across hierarchical layers and jurisdictions. Exploiting the 2008 Brazilian reform of related‐party transaction disclosure as a natural experiment and leveraging a unique dataset covering both publicly traded and privately owned business groups, we show that increased transparency shapes the top layers of the pyramid to maximize security benefits. At the same time, to partially offset the loss of private benefits of control due to increased diversion costs, we find that groups increase the number of offshore affiliates to relocate diversion‐prone activities to jurisdictions with weaker disclosure regimes. These findings contribute to related literature by demonstrating that transparency reforms trigger organizational adaptation across both hierarchical and geographic dimensions.

title: How Do Employees Navigate Destructive Leadership Behaviour? A Focus on SMEs
authors: Afsaneh Bagheri; Safoora Pitsi; Gholamreza Polooee
affiliations: Lincoln International Business School University of Lincoln Lincoln LN6 7TS UK; Excelsia University College Pennant Hills NSW 2120 Australia; University of Wollongong Wollongong NSW 2500 Australia; Faculty of Entrepreneurship University of Tehran Tehran Iran
abstract: Abstract Destructive leadership has detrimental effects on employee and organizational performance, yet we know little about how employees respond to such leadership behaviour, particularly in small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs), where close interpersonal relationships and limited organizational support constrain employees’ responses. Drawing on Leader‐Member Exchange (LMX) theory, we examine the coping strategies employees adopt to navigate destructive leadership behaviour and the mechanisms that shape these strategies. We conducted 26 semi‐structured interviews with employees across diverse SMEs and job roles and analysed the data thematically. We identify three coping strategies: (i) adaptation, (ii) resistance and (iii) exit. Employees’ choice among these strategies depends on their assessment of their tolerance of personal and professional risks and their perceived power to influence or change their situation. These evaluations determine whether employees accommodate their leaders’ destructive behaviour, resist it or disengage entirely by leaving the organization. Our findings extend LMX theory by highlighting employees’ active role in evaluating their interactions and adapting their responses according to the associated risks and their power to influence or change their situation. The study also highlights the contextual dynamics of SMEs and offers insights for organizations seeking to recognize the effects of destructive leadership and support employees.

title: The Costs and Benefits of Guest Worker Programs: Experimental Evidence from the India-UAE Migration Corridor,
authors: Suresh Naidu; Yaw Nyarko; Shing-Yi Wang
affiliations: Columbia University ,; New York University ,; University of Pennsylvania ,
abstract: Abstract We estimate the returns to temporary, legal migration using a randomized experiment with Indian applicants for construction jobs in the UAE. Individuals who migrate doubled their earnings. However, migrants paid substantial upfront costs to labor intermediaries and reported significant falls in well-being. We extrapolate linear marginal treatment effects for workers who declined the offer and find they would have similar pecuniary returns to migration but would experience larger drops in well-being. We estimate that accounting for the fall in well-being and the intermediary costs reduce the welfare gains of temporary migration to the UAE to one-half of the pecuniary gains alone.

title: Successive h-indices using OpenAlex
authors: Nicholas Stearns Selby
abstract: Abstract I apply Schubert’s successive h-index framework to OpenAlex, computing h $$_{2}$$ 2 for 22,980 institutions and h 3 for 214 countries across 13.3 million researchers. The overall institution-level ranking is substantially shaped by biomedical field representation: Medicine accounts for 24% of the author pool and institutions without a large biomedical program are in general structurally disadvantaged, though the overall ranking is not reducible to biomedical representation alone. Field-specific decomposition is more informative: according to this metric, Wageningen University leads Agricultural & Biological Sciences and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences leads Environmental Science, Materials Science, and Engineering; Carnegie Mellon leads Computer Science from 159th; Brazil holds two of the world’s top-six dental-research institutions by field h $$_{2}$$ 2 . I normalize for group size using Egghe’s Lotkaian scaling and find that Italy and Japan tie on h 3 despite a 6 $$\times$$ × difference in institutional scale.

title: Preprints Without Curation Are Increasingly Cited by Journals
authors: Chiaki Miura; Ichiro Sakata
affiliations: Department of Engineering, Technology Management and Innovations, The University of Tokyo, Bunkyo, Tokyo 113-0033, Japan
abstract: Abstract The recent strain on peer review systems necessitates publicizing knowledge before formal review. Citing a preprint was traditionally permitted only if marked as provisional and under review; now, preprints remaining only on servers (non-curated preprints) are cited without such indication. Linking six major preprint servers to the world’s largest bibliographic reference database and restricting to top-journal citations, we compare citation rates with a null model of authors indifferent between preprints and vetted articles. Preprints are cited 5-10 times less often than their share of the literature predicts, yet journal articles are increasingly likely to cite preprints, a rise robust since 2013 and exceeding what exponential submission growth alone would produce. Confounding factors (faster publishing cycles, a few highly cited preprints) cannot explain this shift. Unexpectedly, the COVID-19 pandemic did not amplify this growth but coincided with a deceleration in citation rates. These findings indicate a structural shift in citing behavior: preprints are increasingly perceived as credible regardless of later publication status, motivating attention to how citation conventions and journal policies should accommodate their expanding role. Our evidence comes from biology, where preprint adoption has expanded rapidly beyond arXiv’s strongholds of physics and mathematics; generalizability to other disciplines remains open.

title: The Geography of Nobel Prize Nomination, 1901–1975
authors: Chad M. Topaz; Anvi Kurongonayini; Bennett Ptak; Arden Fluehr; Ariana Mendible; Rachel Roca; Nancy Rodríguez; Lu Xian; Régan Schwartz; Jude Higdon
affiliations: QSIDE Institute; Williams College; University of Colorado–Boulder; Seattle University; Michigan State University; University of Michigan; Bennington College
abstract: Abstract Nobel laureates are concentrated in a few countries, yet where geographic sorting enters the prize’s selection pipeline remains unknown. From archival, parliamentary, and web sources we construct a five-layer network built around the nomination records of five prizes, 1901–1975, with 512,793 edges and 8,133 identified participants. Although Swedish and Norwegian bodies administer the prizes, the nominators who actually took part were geographically diverse. Within that pool, however, nominators chose same-country nominees 4.85 times as often as random matching would predict. This homophily ratio ranges by discipline from 8.58 in Literature to 3.01 in Physics. With matching restricted to the same prize and year, the ratio is still 3.3. The continent-level ratio rose through the 1940s and stayed elevated as the nominee pool kept diversifying. A model that adjusts for how many nominations each country sent and received yields a roughly fifteenfold same-country premium, still sevenfold after adjusting for shared language. Nominations that crossed geographic regions flowed asymmetrically, with Northern America the dominant net importer. A nominee’s same-country nomination share was negatively associated with eventually winning the prize. In sum, across the stages we can observe, geographic sorting concentrates at the discretionary nomination decision, beyond what the nominator pool’s composition predicts.

title: Multi-source, multi-level, graph-based institutional collaboration indicators for research assessment with Ricgraph
authors: Rik D.T. Janssen
affiliations: Utrecht University, Utrecht, the Netherlands
abstract: Abstract Researchers rarely work alone: they work with colleagues within and between organizations on all organizational levels. They collaborate on a variety of research results beyond traditional publications. However, collaboration indicators in research assessment usually rely on a single source, focus on top-level institutions, and may focus on journal articles only. This limits what can be seen about collaborations within organizations, and for results such as data sets and software. This article introduces a multi-source, multi-level, graph-based approach to collaboration indicators using Ricgraph (Research in context graph). Publications, data sets, software, persons, and organizational information from multiple systems are integrated into a single graph. Collaborations are defined as shared research results connecting organizations via persons. They are quantified on top-level organization, as well as on faculty and departmental level, providing a concrete operationalization of multi-source, multi-level collaboration indicators for science-of-science research. Combining multiple sources substantially increases the observed coverage of collaborations, especially for data set and software collaborations (>400% for sources in this article, compared to a single source). Multi-level collaborations overviews reveal patterns that are invisible at the top-level alone. These results illustrate how multi-source, multi-level, graph-based collaboration indicators can complement citation-based metrics in responsible research assessment and institutional evaluation.

title: Between Policy and Proposal: A Quantitative Analysis of Research Data Management in DFG Individual Grants (2017–2025)
authors: Richard Heidler; Jan Rohden; Christoph Funk
affiliations: Information Management, Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, Germany; Scientific Library Services and Information Systems, Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft, Germany
abstract: Abstract Research funding agencies increasingly require researchers to describe how they will manage and share research data, yet little is known about how such policy requirements are reflected in grant proposals. This paper examines how research data management (RDM) is documented in proposals submitted to the German Research Foundation’s (DFG) Individual Research Grants Program between 2017 and 2025, and how these descriptions evolve over time and across disciplines. To address this question, we combine Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML), and repository linking to analyze a large corpus of proposal texts. This approach enables a systematic assessment of RDM sections and the identification of referenced repositories. The results show growing awareness of RDM, reflected in longer, more substantive statements and increasing repository references. We also find disciplinary differences in how RDM is articulated, pointing to varying levels of maturity across fields. A marked shift in proposal documentation following the introduction of a DFG checklist in 2021 suggests that policy instruments are associated with changes in how RDM is documented in proposals. Overall, the findings indicate that funding agencies may shape how RDM is articulated in proposals through guidance-based approaches, providing insights into the monitoring and design of Open Science policies.

title: Collateral Demand in Wholesale Funding Markets
authors: Jamie Coen; Patrick Coen; Anne-Caroline Hüser
affiliations: Imperial College London , U.K; Warwick Business School , U.K; Bank of England , U.K
abstract: Abstract Repo markets are systemically important funding markets, but are also used by firms to obtain the assets provided as collateral. We build and structurally estimate a model of trade between heterogeneous firms in the sterling gilt repo market, and show that this collateral demand depresses repo market activity and can impede the transmission of monetary policy. We quantify how well-designed central bank repo facilities can improve outcomes: if the central bank were to lend out the assets on its balance sheet following quantitative easing, transmission and total firm surplus would improve by 20% and 38%, respectively.

title: Hedging by Giving: Spiritual Insurance and Religious Donations
authors: Yu-Jane Liu; Juanjuan Meng; Dalin Sheng; Guangxin Yang; Yu Zhang
affiliations: Peking University Guanghua School of Management; Southwestern University of Finance and Economics China Center for Behavioral Economics and Finance; Xiamen University School of Management
abstract: Abstract We investigate “spiritual insurance”—a mental strategy for coping with risk, where individuals engage in good deeds, including donations, in exchange for perceived blessings and protection. Using bank transactional data, we show that higher income uncertainty and health shocks lead to increased donations, particularly to religious charities. Moreover, individuals who donate to religious charities tend to reduce insurance expenditures. In a field experiment on millions of potential donors through an online platform, we find that spiritual insurance narratives increase giving, providing direct causal evidence for such a motive. Our findings provide new evidence on how spiritual insurance affects household risk-coping behavior.
